title: Building for Earthquakes
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Engineers have a saying that earthquakes do not kill people; buildings do. In most major earthquakes, the great majority of deaths are caused not by the shaking of the ground itself but by the collapse of structures on the people inside them. Two buildings standing side by side may experience exactly the same movement, yet one may be left with nothing worse than cracked plaster while the other falls in a heap. The aim of earthquake engineering is therefore not to prevent all damage, which would be prohibitively expensive, but to make sure that a building stays standing long enough for the people inside to get out.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some traditional structures achieved this long before the science was understood. Japan's tall wooden pagodas, some of them more than a thousand years old, have survived centuries of earthquakes that destroyed the buildings around them, and very few are recorded as having collapsed. Each storey rests loosely on the one below rather than being rigidly fixed to it, so that during an earthquake the storeys sway in different directions, in a movement that has been compared to the slithering of a snake. Many pagodas also have a heavy central pillar running through the middle of the structure. Exactly how much this pillar contributes is still debated, but it may act as a kind of spine that stops the storeys from moving too far.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The key quality of a modern earthquake-resistant building is ductility – the ability to bend and stretch without breaking. Concrete is strong when it is squeezed but brittle when it is pulled or bent, so in earthquake zones it must be reinforced with enough steel bars, carefully placed, to hold it together as it cracks. Engineers also follow a principle sometimes summarised as 'strong columns, weak beams'. If something has to fail, it should be the horizontal beams, which can be badly damaged without bringing the building down, rather than the vertical columns that hold up every floor above them. When columns fail first, the floors can collapse one on top of another, leaving almost no space for survivors.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A more radical approach is to separate the building from the ground altogether. In a technique called base isolation, the structure sits not directly on its foundations but on a set of bearings made from alternating layers of rubber and steel. The bearings are stiff vertically, so they can carry the building's weight, but flexible horizontally, so that when the ground moves sideways the building above moves much more slowly and gently. Base isolation is expensive, and is mostly used for buildings that must continue to function after an earthquake, such as hospitals and emergency control centres. It also works best for low and medium-rise buildings rather than very tall ones.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Tall towers often rely instead on a device known as a tuned mass damper. The best-known example hangs near the top of Taipei 101 in Taiwan: a steel sphere weighing around 660 tonnes, suspended from cables. When the tower sways, the sphere swings in the opposite direction, absorbing part of the motion. Although the damper was designed mainly to reduce the swaying caused by typhoon winds, it also helps during earthquakes, and it has become a tourist attraction in its own right, with its own viewing area.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Impressive as these technologies are, they do little for the millions of people who live in buildings that already exist. For most cities, the greater challenge is retrofitting – strengthening older buildings that were constructed before modern standards applied. Some of the most dangerous are so-called soft-storey buildings, in which the ground floor consists mainly of open space, such as a car park or a row of shop windows, with the weight of several floors of flats resting on a few thin columns. In 2015 the city of Los Angeles made it compulsory for owners of thousands of such buildings to strengthen them, usually by adding steel frames at ground level. The cost was shared between owners and tenants.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In poorer countries, where many houses are built by their owners without engineers, the most effective measures are often the simplest. Researchers working after major earthquakes in South Asia found that the way walls were tied together mattered more than the materials themselves. A continuous horizontal band of reinforced concrete or timber running around the top of a brick or stone wall, for instance, can stop the corners from separating during shaking, at a cost of only a small percentage of the price of the house. The engineer Sunita Rao, who has trained builders in rural Nepal, argues that 'the most important earthquake technology is not a machine but a mason who knows why each detail matters'.

items.text: a reference to how the cost of a safety measure was divided
an explanation of why it is not realistic to prevent all damage
a description of a technique that suits some building heights better than others
an example of a building feature whose purpose is not fully understood
a claim that training people is more important than equipment

groups.limit: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.title: Making concrete buildings safer

rows.text: Concrete performs well under pressure but is {23} when bent, so it needs steel reinforcement. A good earthquake-resistant building has {24}, meaning that it can bend without breaking. If the columns give way before the beams, the floors may fall onto each other and leave little room for {25}. Older buildings with an open ground floor, known as {26} buildings, are particularly at risk.
